title: SYSK Selects: Can you Treat Mental Illness with Psychedelics?
summary: SYSK Selects episode chosen by Josh, presenting a past episode on whether psychedelics can treat mental illness. The hosts trace the history of LSD, MDMA (ecstasy), and psilocybin: early CIA and British experiments, Alexander Shulgin's MDMA work, Dr. Oscar Janiger-era and Hollywood psychiatrist Mortimer Hartman's Beverly Hills LSD sessions with celebrities like Cary Grant, Esther Williams, and Aldous Huxley, and Time magazine's favorable coverage. They cover the outlawing of LSD and MDMA, Timothy Leary's role in public backlash, and George Ricaurte's retracted study that falsely linked MDMA to brain damage, which fed into the RAVE Act. Modern research in Switzerland, Johns Hopkins, UCLA, and elsewhere shows promising results for PTSD, depression, cluster headaches, end-of-life anxiety, and addiction (ibogaine), with serotonin as a likely mechanism. The episode closes with Bill W.'s LSD interest, reflections on legal versus illegal drugs, and listener mail about octopuses.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick on treating mental illness with psychedelics. The hosts banter about LSD, Albert Hofmann's discovery, MDMA's origins, and the history of these drugs being legal, then outlawed.

segments.title: Early government and Shulgin's MDMA work
segments.summary: The hosts note British MI6 and Canadian government LSD experiments and the CIA's dosing experiments. They discuss MDMA's creation in 1914 and Alexander Shulgin's publication on its effects, and how it spread among psychiatrists and into Dallas clubs.

segments.title: Hollywood LSD sessions in Beverly Hills
segments.summary: Mortimer Hartman and Arthur Chandler ran the Psychiatric Institute of Beverly Hills, offering LSD sessions from Sandoz. Aldous Huxley, Charles Brackett, Cary Grant, and Claire Booth Luce are mentioned, and Time and Look magazine and Good Housekeeping published favorable coverage.

segments.title: Esther Williams' LSD experience
segments.summary: Esther Williams took LSD at Hartman's office after a referral from Cary Grant. She describes a jarring mirror experience involving her late brother, which the hosts discuss as an example of breakthroughs.

segments.title: Outlawing of LSD and MDMA; George Ricaurte
segments.summary: LSD was outlawed around 1965 and the Beverly Hills shop closed by 1970. The hosts describe how Dr. George Ricaurte published a study claiming MDMA causes permanent brain damage, which fed into scheduling and the RAVE Act, until his monkey study was found to have used methamphetamine and was retracted from Science.

segments.title: Timothy Leary and the backlash
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Timothy Leary's advocacy for LSD, which they say contributed to public backlash and the end of medical LSD research, and how the NIDA fact sheet on ecstasy was pulled after the retraction.

segments.title: Modern psychedelic research for mental illness
segments.summary: Researchers in Switzerland, Los Angeles, Johns Hopkins, and UCLA are studying LSD, psilocybin, MDMA, and ketamine. Results include a PTSD study where ten of twelve patients no longer met diagnostic criteria, and benefits for depression, cluster headaches, and OCD. Serotonin is discussed as a likely mechanism, and the hosts explain why these drugs are not seen as addictive.

segments.title: Lower doses, a happy pill, and LSD risks
segments.summary: The hosts note that trial psilocybin doses are likely low, debate whether they would take a legal happy pill, cite a BBC survey where 70 percent said they would not, and mention that LSD can worsen mental illness, citing Brian Wilson and Syd Barrett.

segments.title: Pamela Sukhdeo's end-of-life psilocybin case and ibogaine
segments.summary: The hosts describe Pamela Secuda, a colon cancer patient in a UCLA psilocybin study, whose anxiety eased and who lived more fully before dying in 2006. They then describe ibogaine's use in breaking opioid and cocaine addiction with reduced withdrawal symptoms.

segments.title: Bill Wilson, legal versus illegal drugs
segments.summary: The hosts describe Alcoholics Anonymous co-founder Bill Wilson's LSD use in the 1950s and how it may aid the twelve-step reflection process. They then reflect on why alcohol is legal while other drugs are not, and how public sentiment shapes these views.

segments.title: Listener mail on octopuses and outro
segments.summary: A listener who works as an aquarist describes octopus enrichment work and a two spot octopus learning to open a jar. The hosts close with a family saying from a listener's father and a sign-off.
